match.reason: Neither bank point teaches the brief's three-step split of drafting, editing for ideas and structure, and a separate final proofreading step for spelling, punctuation and grammar. The first point folds spelling into editing and adds planning and publishing, and the second is Year 11 depth with a separate revising step.

draft.title: Drafting, editing and proofreading
card: Get your ideas down on the page. Do not stop to fix every spelling slip. The aim is a first version you can work with.
Improve the writing itself. Check that the ideas are clear, the order makes sense and the words are well chosen. You may move, cut or add whole sentences.
Check the small errors in spelling, punctuation and grammar. Do this last, once the content is settled, so you do not fix sentences you later delete.
The order matters: draft, then edit, then proofread. Reading your work aloud can help you spot problems at both of the later steps.
draft.remember: Draft to get ideas down, edit to improve them, proofread last to catch small errors.

a.q: Sam has finished a first version of his story. He now swaps two paragraphs and replaces a dull verb. Which step is he doing?
a.why: Moving paragraphs and changing word choice improve the structure and the words, which is editing. Proofreading is tempting, but it only fixes spelling, punctuation and grammar errors.
a.clue: He is changing order and word choice, not small errors.

b.q: Priya has edited her speech and is happy with its ideas and order. What should she do next, and why?
opts: Proofread it, because the content is now settled
Draft it again, because the ideas need to be fixed
Proofread it first, then edit the order of ideas
Edit it again, because spelling is part of editing
b.why: Proofreading comes last, once the content is settled, so she does not correct sentences she might later change. Proofreading before editing is tempting, but it can waste effort on text that gets cut or moved.

b.best: Proofread it, because the content is now settled
